messages.subject: initial values problem with truncated poisson (partly rstan)
parts:
While trying to estimate a model with a truncated poisson distribution I
got
Initialization failed after 100 attempts. Try specifying initial
values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the
model.

I got this for all 3 chains in the production run, though I did not get
it in my initial trial run with a different seed.

This was with development code c Sep 12 (currently running more recent
code, but busy with the multinomial).

It didn't seem too much could go wrong, and so I was surprised by the
difficulties. Perhaps largish value of the linear parameter are causing
trouble when exponentiated? I gave the first parameter a uniform prior
on [-5, 5], and exp(5) might be too much.

Several questions or issues:
1) Exactly how does stan generate random initial values? I can't find
much about it, though I thought I saw that they were drawn from [0, 2].

2) Is there a way to find more precisely what is failing?

3) Have I made some goof in my model?

4) I don't relish generating a set of over-dispersed values for my
parameters on my own. The R documentation is a tad opaque; in
particular I'm not sure what this option for init means:
"a list of initial parameter values with
which to indicate how the initial values of parameters are
specified"
It sounds very meta.

BTW there is a typo at the end of the R help for the init parameter of
stan: "lenght "

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

Model:
data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
int<lower=0> J; //number of covariates
int<lower=0> NSD; // number of classes of beta for sd
int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J]; // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
int<lower=0> NCLUSTER; //number of respondents
int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
matrix[N, J] x; // covariates
int<lower=1,upper=15> nDetail[N]; // outcome
}
parameters {
vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
real<lower=0> sigma;
real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
vector[J] beta;
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
for(ir in 1:J) {
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
}
alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma;
}
model {
vector[N] beta_x;
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
for (j in 2:J) {
beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
}
alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
for (n in 1:N) {
beta_x[n] <- (x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]];
//truncated poisson can't be vectorized
// and is not available in log form
nDetail[n] ~ poisson(exp(beta_x[n])) T[1, 15];
}
}

> difficulties. Perhaps largish value of the linear parameter are causing
> trouble when exponentiated? I gave the first parameter a uniform prior
> on [-5, 5], and exp(5) might be too much.

It's 150 --- is that too much? Is 1/150 too little?

You can try with init=0 and see if that works.

> Several questions or issues:
> 1) Exactly how does stan generate random initial values? I can't find
> much about it, though I thought I saw that they were drawn from [0, 2].

The random initial values are drawn uniformly from [-2,2] on
the unconstrained scale. The transforms are in the transform chapter.

I'll add more to the doc.
> 2) Is there a way to find more precisely what is failing?

You can evaluate the gradients using test_grad=TRUE on the
Stan call. That'll evaluate the log prob and gradients at
your init values (given by you or randomly initialized or
initialized to 0).

You can print as you go. What causes it to fail is a -infinity
or NaN value. You can get those, for instance, if you provide
variables outside of the support of a distribution, or if there
are underflows or overflows in arithmetic.
> 3) Have I made some goof in my model?

Not that I can see.

It looks like your data declaration matches the truncation.

The exp() is the most likely thing to cause overflow/underflow problems.
In general, you should worry if you need exp() of large values.

> 4) I don't relish generating a set of over-dispersed values for my
> parameters on my own.
It's just the parameters:

> parameters {
> vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
> vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
> }

That'd be easy to generate in R -- they all have either
cauchy, normal, or uniform distributions.

> The R documentation is a tad opaque; in
> particular I'm not sure what this option for init means:
> "a list of initial parameter values with
> which to indicate how the initial values of parameters are
> specified"
> It sounds very meta.

:-) I think it's more redundant than meta. The usual thing
to pass in is a function that returns a list of parameter values.
You might be able to pass in a plain old list.

- Bob

I tried a much simpler truncated poisson model on the same data: only an
intercept and cluster effects. The trial results suggest an awkward
fit:

1 chains, each with iter=200; warmup=100; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=100, total post-warmup draws=100.

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
beta -5.3 0 0.1 -5.4 -5.3 -5.3 -5.2 -5.1 15 1.0
sigma 4.1 0 0.0 4.0 4.1 4.1 4.2 4.2 9 1.1
sigma_beta 1.4 0 0.0 1.4 1.4 1.4 1.4 1.4 7 1.0

beta is the intercept; sigma the variance for clusters; and sigma_beta
the variance for beta (in the prior--obviously the posterior is qutie
tight).

Since exp(beta) ~ 0 this means the corresponding (pre-truncation)
poisson is mostly zero, and the relevant part in [1, 15] is from the
tail. So the counts are a mixture of those and some clusters which have
mean value substantially > 0.

I think I need a different model, but I'm not sure what.

There are 737 observations with 351 clusters; many of the clusters are
singletons, but a few are large (like around 100 members).

I'm running more iterations to check.

parts:
On Fri, 2013-10-18 at 12:47 -0700, Ross Boylan wrote:
> Since exp(beta) ~ 0 this means the corresponding (pre-truncation)
> poisson is mostly zero, and the relevant part in [1, 15] is from the
> tail. So the counts are a mixture of those and some clusters which
> have
> mean value substantially > 0.

I think the model is saying there are a lot of observations of 1, and I
should use a "1-inflated" distribution.

From http://mathworld.wolfram.com/PoissonDistribution.html equation 10,
p(i+i)/p(i) = mean/(i+1)

So as the mean approaches zero essentially all the mass will be on the
first point in the allowed range, 1.

This makes the predictions a whole bunch of 1's and then some "real"
poissons.

I could just model n-1 and be done with the lower bound. This seems
kind of wrong; there are 0's out in the world, but our sample doesn't
include them by design. Maybe the shortcut will be bad in theory but
good in practice.

Ross

I'd always suggest starting by plotting the data. If the data
doesn't fit a Poisson, then clearly that's not going to work.

Sometimes you just need more (and sometimes less) variance and can get that
with a negative binomial.

Or you can build mixture models like a zero-inflated or
1-inflated Poisson. There's a note on how to do that for the Poisson
in our appendix on BUGS vs. Stan. But is the residual data Poisson
after removing the 1 inflation?

- Bob

The negative binomial IS a Poisson mixture model:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution#Gamma.E2.80.93Poisson_mixture

Using negative binomial should be more efficient because it
integrates out the intermediate gamma-distributed mean parameter
analytically.

No, it won't be. If you find yourself reusing expensive caclculations
like this, it helps to

There's a poisson_log distribution that should let you avoid the exp(beta_x[n])
inside the poisson. I hope the new manual is a little clearer on names.
In your case, you'd call poisson_log_log(0,beta_x[n]).

Also, I don't think the whole censoring thing is being done right here.
You need a mixture of censored vs. uncensored here, so I think you need
to add the poisson_cdf to the other calcs. That's more a modeling issue
than a Stan issue, though.

- Bob

terms; so it is still getting mulitplied by (sum in logs) .

This is inefficient since poisson(9) + poisson_ccdf(9) =
poisson_ccdf(8)
assuming poisson_ccdf(n) = 1 - poisson_cdf(n), i.e., it is the number
strictly greater than n. With that one adjustment I think that's
increment_log_prob(bernouill(0) + poissson_ccdf(8))
which is yours, except an off by 1.

One subtlety is that what's being modeled as poisson is the number of
partners - 1, so the number for 10 partners is from the distribution
for 9 or more.

>>> used look like this one. The probability of the top category (10) is
>>> just the regular probability of 10 + the probability of any higher
>>> value. That is, if someone has a true value of 23, they will report
>>> 10.
>>
>> It still doesn't look right to me, but I'm often wrong about these
>> things as I'm still an amateur statistician.
>>
>> For your one-inflated model, I've reformatted to remove tabs and
>> make it clearer:
>>
>> if (mnDetail[n] == 1)
>> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_log(1, theta),
>> bernoulli_log(0, theta)
>> + poisson_log(0, exp(beta_x[n]))));
>> else {
>> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0, theta)
>> + poisson_log(mnDetail[n]-1, exp(beta_x[n])));
>> if (mnDetail[n] == 10)
>> increment_log_prob(poisson_ccdf_log(9, exp(beta_x[n])));
>> }
>>
>> In the else condition, I think you really want this:
>>
>> else if (mnDetail[n] == 10)
>> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0,theta)
>> + poisson_ccdf_log(9, exp(beta_x[n])));
>> else
>> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0, theta)
>> + poisson_log(mnDetail[n]-1, exp(beta_x[n])));
>>
>> I didn't check the bounds of 9 vs. 10 and what not, but I think you
>> need the bernoulli_log(0,theta) in there for the other cases because
>> of the mixture.
>>
>> But as I said, if I'm wrong, it wouldn't be the first time!
>>
> I think the bernoulli_log(0) is already there.
> If mnDetail[n] == 10 the original code does
> (since mnDetail[n]-1 = 9)
> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0, theta) + poisson_log(9, exp(beta_x[n])))
> and then
> increment_log_prob(poisson_ccdf(9), exp((beta_x[n])))
> which I think is equivalent to increment_log_prob of the sum of the 3
> terms; so it is still getting mulitplied by (sum in logs) .
>
> This is inefficient since poisson(9) + poisson_ccdf(9) =
> poisson_ccdf(8)
> assuming poisson_ccdf(n) = 1 - poisson_cdf(n), i.e., it is the number
> strictly greater than n. With that one adjustment I think that's
> increment_log_prob(bernouill(0) + poissson_ccdf(8))
> which is yours, except an off by 1.


> One subtlety is that what's being modeled as poisson is the number of
> partners - 1, so the number for 10 partners is from the distribution
> for 9 or more.

I see --- thanks for explaining. A comment in the code for
something this tricky would help readers like me.

The way I coded it would be more efficient, and it'd be
clearer to me, but this kind of thing's often in the eye of
the author.

- Bob
